title: Why Do We Call a Computer Fault a Bug? The Word Is Older Than the Moth
parts: Your computer has a bug.
Nobody has ever seen it.
Everyone says the word comes from a moth.
Is that true?
Let's follow the evidence.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
First, the moth.
On September ninth, nineteen forty-seven, a team at Harvard reported a moth caught between relay contacts in the Mark Two computer.
Our reading: a relay is a small electric switch, and a moth between its contacts can stop it from closing.
The team taped the moth into the logbook.
Beside it they wrote: first actual case of bug being found.
The logbook, moth still attached, is now at the Smithsonian.
So the moth story is documented.
Now look at that sentence again.
First actual case of bug being found.
Our reading: if that is a joke, it only works if everyone already knew the word.
Writer Michael Quinion says the entry implies the word was already common.
Grace Hopper made the incident famous in her lectures, says the Computer History Museum.
But the Smithsonian says the logbook was probably not hers.
So how old is the word?
Go back to nineteen forty-five.
Wikipedia says the Oxford English Dictionary cites a journal article that uses debug for engine testing.
A nineteen forty-four letter from Robert Oppenheimer uses the word debugging, Wikipedia adds.
In a story that same year, Isaac Asimov used bug for robot malfunctions.
Our reading: you can only debug something that has bugs.
Now go back further, to eighteen seventy-eight.
Thomas Edison wrote a letter to a business associate.
Wikipedia quotes him saying that such little faults and difficulties are called bugs.
That is almost seventy years before the moth.
In eighteen eighty-nine, a London newspaper, the Pall Mall Gazette, described Edison hunting a bug in his phonograph.
Edison using the word is documented.
So did Edison invent the word?
I triple E Spectrum says he coined it.
Wikipedia calls it engineering jargon since at least the eighteen seventies.
Quinion suggests the word pictures a hidden, imaginary insect causing trouble.
Where the word really comes from is still open.
So let us count.
The moth, the logbook, and the note: documented.
Edison using bug for faults in eighteen seventy-eight: documented.
Edison coined the word: disputed.
The moth gave us the word: myth.
Our reading: computing borrowed it. Wikipedia notes that two nineteen fifty-two computing papers still put debugging in quotation marks.
Our reading: the moth did not invent the word. It made a good story famous.
Next time you call a fault a bug, you are using a word older than electronic computers.
So here is a last question.
Which everyday word do you use without knowing where it comes from?
